description: Uncertain entries of the world model: `entry` names the fact left open ({of, attr, time}; `of` "?" when the question is who). `raised`: the paragraph (and quote) where the story opens it; null while the story never doubts it (`latent`). `possibilities`: every answer the story makes available, each `{value, how?, available, via, from?, quote?, out?, by?}`. `available` is the paragraph from which the answer may be listed; `via` is `direct` (the story names it as a possibility), `indirect` (it follows from what has been told, or a careful reader's thought: `from` a fact or "thought t<id>") or `always` ("something else", on every question from the paragraph it is raised). `quote` is the words that make it available, found in that paragraph (for answers that become available after the facts so far run out). `out`/`by`: the paragraph and fact that rule it out. `answer` is always one of the possibilities, or null where the story never settles it. `answer_inferable_at` (with `answer_from`, a fact or thought, and `answer_strength: likely` when a careful reader would hold it but it does not follow strictly) is the earliest paragraph a reader can reach the answer, null when only the give-away brings it; `answer_given_at`/`answer_given_quote` where the story gives it away. `old`: the old game's question or slot.

questions.label: What did the stranger want at the stable?
questions.quote: Can you tell me where I am?
questions.answer_given_quote: Therefore Simpson becomes eliminated from the case

questions.label: What was in the stranger's paper?
questions.quote: He took a piece of white paper folded up out of his waistcoat pocket
questions.answer_given_quote: He says that it was a ten-pound note
questions.note: A ten-pound note (the old game's ten_pound_note).

questions.label: Who was the stranger?
questions.quote: a man appeared out of the darkness
questions.answer_given_quote: He did not attempt to deny that he had acted as described upon the evening before

questions.label: Where did the stranger go after the stable?
questions.quote: he was gone

possibilities.how: back in the night, as the police think

questions.note: The story never accounts for his night beyond the wet clothes; the old game leaves it open.

questions.label: Who drugged Hunter's supper?
questions.quote: Hunter was obviously under the influence of some powerful drug
questions.answer_given_quote: why should he drug his own stable-boy?
questions.note: From ¶37 every member of the household (f.member_household_*) is available: the dish was drugged after his portion was set apart.

questions.label: Where was the opium put into the supper?
questions.quote: contain an appreciable quantity of powdered opium

possibilities.value: on the path, by the maid
at the window, by the stranger
at the house, after his portion was set apart

questions.answer: at the house, after his portion was set apart
questions.answer_given_quote: The opium was added after the dish was set aside for the stable-boy

questions.label: Did the dog bark in the night?
questions.quote: They had heard nothing during the night
questions.answer_given_quote: The dog did nothing in the night-time.
questions.note: The story does not raise it by ¶46; the careful reader does (t34.4). The dog's silence becomes Holmes's point much later.

questions.label: Who opened the stable door in the night?
questions.quote: The door was open
questions.answer_given_quote: John Straker went down to the stables in the dead of the night and took out Silver Blaze
questions.note: The key and who holds it are not told by ¶46; the trainer's key is the reader's assumption.

questions.label: Who led Silver Blaze out of the stable?

entry.value: leading Silver Blaze out of the stable

questions.quote: the favourite’s stall was empty

possibilities.how: the horse got out by himself

questions.answer_given_quote: John Straker went down to the stables in the dead of the night and took out Silver Blaze

questions.label: Why did Straker go out at one in the morning?
questions.quote: he said that he could not sleep on account of his anxiety about the horses

possibilities.value: to see that all was well
to take the horse out for early exercise

possibilities.note: Named directly at ¶57 ("If he wished to injure it", of Simpson); laming at ¶173.

questions.answer_given_quote: it is possible to make a slight nick upon the tendons of a horse’s ham

questions.label: Was Straker honest?
questions.answer_given_quote: John Straker was a man who was entirely unworthy of your confidence
questions.note: Reported as character; the story never doubts it by ¶46, a careful reader may (t46.7).

questions.label: How did Straker's overcoat come to the furze-bush?

entry.how: how it came to the furze-bush

questions.quote: John Straker’s overcoat was flapping from a furze-bush
questions.answer_given_quote: He had already, in spite of the rain, taken off his overcoat
questions.note: To work (what work is given much later). ¶96–97 settle that it was placed, not by whom.

questions.label: Who struck the blow that killed Straker?

entry.value: striking the blow that shattered Straker's head

questions.quote: the tragic murder of its trainer
questions.answer_given_quote: The real murderer is standing immediately behind you
questions.note: Watson's narration says 'murder' (¶4); the horse is available only to a careful reader (t37.13).

questions.label: What made the blow to Straker's head?

entry.value: the heavy weapon of the blow

questions.quote: a savage blow from some heavy weapon
questions.answer_given_quote: the steel shoe had struck Straker full on the forehead
questions.note: The horse's steel shoe.

questions.label: What made the cut on Straker's thigh?

entry.value: what made the cut on Straker's thigh

questions.quote: a long, clean cut, inflicted evidently by some very sharp instrument
questions.answer_given_quote: his knife gashed his thigh
questions.note: Holmes calls Watson's suggestion probable (¶44); the mechanism Watson gives (convulsions) is not the answer's.

questions.label: Did Straker fight a man in the hollow?
questions.quote: one at least of his assailants must bear his mark upon him
questions.answer_given_quote: had lashed out, and the steel shoe had struck Straker
questions.note: Told as fact at ¶35; ¶41 (no wound on Simpson) and ¶43–44 (his own knife) open it.

questions.label: How did the cravat come into Straker's hand?

entry.how: how it came into Straker's hand

questions.quote: was utterly unable to account for its presence in the hand of the murdered man

possibilities.value: torn from the stranger in the struggle
lost by the stranger, picked up by Straker

questions.answer: lost by the stranger, picked up by Straker
questions.answer_given_quote: Simpson in his flight had dropped his cravat, and Straker had picked it up

questions.label: Where is Silver Blaze?
questions.quote: the most remarkable horse in England could long remain concealed

possibilities.value: dead, in a pit or mine

possibilities.how: hidden among horses at a stable

questions.answer_given_quote: He tried to bluster out of it, but I described to him so exactly what his actions had been
questions.note: 'Loose on the moor' strains against the gypsies' watch and the reward (¶37). Holmes argues it and the gypsies out at ¶114; that is argument, not proof.

questions.label: Who gave the papers their account of the night?
questions.note: How the papers had the night's events is never said.

questions.label: Where did Holmes get his account of the case?
questions.note: Holmes read every paper; whether Gregory's telegram told him more is not said.

questions.label: Who answered Holmes's wire?
questions.note: Both had wired Holmes on Tuesday (¶12).

questions.label: What was Straker's knife for?
questions.quote: A strange thing for a man to carry with him upon a rough expedition
questions.answer_given_quote: And it was to be used for a delicate operation that night

questions.label: Who is William Derbyshire?
questions.quote: made out by Madame Lesurier, of Bond Street, to William Derbyshire
questions.answer_given_quote: who had recognised Straker as an excellent customer of the name of Derbyshire

questions.label: Who is the Madam Derbyshire of the bill?
questions.quote: Madam Derbyshire had somewhat expensive tastes
questions.answer_given_quote: who had a very dashing wife, with a strong partiality for expensive dresses
questions.note: 'Ruled out' at ¶92 only as far as her denial is believed; the costume Holmes names is his own guess from the bill.

questions.label: Why was a match struck in the hollow?

entry.value: why a match was struck in the hollow

questions.quote: It was a wax vesta half burned

possibilities.value: to light the candle for close work

questions.answer: to light the candle for close work
questions.answer_given_quote: Of course that was why he needed the candle, and struck the match

questions.label: Whose track is beside the horse's?
questions.quote: A man’s track was visible beside the horse’s
questions.answer_given_quote: his own boots exactly corresponded to them

questions.label: What did the man with the horse mean to do?
questions.quote: the same tracks coming back again in the opposite direction

possibilities.value: to lead the horse home to King's Pyland, then to hide him
to hide the horse from the start

questions.answer: to lead the horse home to King's Pyland, then to hide him
questions.answer_given_quote: how his first impulse had been to lead him back to King’s Pyland
questions.note: His aim changed at the turn (the old game's split of w.tue_dawn).

questions.label: Were the horse's looks changed?
questions.quote: Should I change it first or not?
questions.answer_given_quote: You have only to wash his face and his leg in spirits of wine
questions.note: The reading audit puts the earliest reach at ¶64 (expert), before the question is raised.

questions.label: What lamed the sheep?
questions.quote: three of them have gone lame
questions.answer_given_quote: showed that my surmise was correct
questions.note: Straker practised the nick on them; the audit's earliest reach (¶92, expert) is before the sheep appear.

questions.label: What is the bay in Ross's colours?
questions.quote: a powerful bay horse swept out from the weighing enclosure
questions.answer_given_quote: he is the same old Silver Blaze as ever
questions.note: With Brown's "Should I change it first?" (¶140) and Ross's "we scratched our other one" (¶192), only Silver Blaze could be in his colours.

questions.label: What drove Straker to it?
questions.quote: John Straker was a man who was entirely unworthy of your confidence

possibilities.value: to win his bets by laying against his own horse

questions.answer_given_quote: this woman had plunged him over head and ears in debt, and so led him into this miserable plot
questions.note: The two possibilities are not exclusive: the debts are the motive, laying against the horse the means (¶220).
